Beyond Latin
  Most typographic advice is advice about Latin. This is which parts of it come from the eye, which parts are Latin-only conventions, and what other writing systems do instead.

  
    Termnon-Latin typography / multiscript typesetting
    Also calledmultiscript typography, world scripts, non-Latin type, international typesetting
    Not the same astranslation vs typesetting, right-to-left vs mirrored layout, vertical text vs rotated text
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Arabic: the letters joinJustification without word spacesDirection is not one arrowJapanese: no word spaces at allAnnotations Latin has no equivalent ofRules that do not transferCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Everything in the three articles before this one was about Latin. X-height, italic, word spaces, 45–75 characters a line. None of it was labelled that way, and that is the problem: the advice gets repeated as though it were about reading, when much of it is about one alphabet only.
Some generalises, because it comes from the eye: a return jump that is too long is unreliable in any script. Much does not, because it comes from Latin letters being separate, proportional, bicameral and left-to-right. Change one of those and the rule evaporates.
Arabic: the letters join
The Arabic script is cursive. ALREQ says it plainly under Cursive text: letters join to their neighbours. So a letter has no single shape — under Joining Forms, each has one, two or four joining forms, decided by what sits either side.



W3C, Arabic & Persian Layout Requirements, §Cursive text → Joining Forms. Reproduced under the W3C Document License: "W3C liability, trademark and permissive document license rules apply."
One letter — meem — four glyphs. Not four styles to choose between: software has to pick the right one from context. The initial form joins leftwards only, the medial joins on both sides, the final joins rightwards only. ALREQ also defines right-joining letters with only two forms, and non-joining letters with one.


ALREQ's Fonts & font styles counts the alphabet at 28 letters, 29 with the hamzah, then concludes that Arabic fonts "typically contain hundreds of glyphs," contemporary ones reaching "many hundreds, in some cases even thousands." Alphabet size tells you nothing about font size.
Justification without word spaces
Latin justifies a line with one lever: stretch and squeeze the spaces between words. ALREQ's Text alignment & justification counts six mechanisms in Arabic, and inter-word spacing is merely the first — the document notes it "is the same mechanism widely used when justifying Latin scripts." The others: gaps inside words at letters that do not join leftwards; wider alternative shapes; ligatures; kashida, stretching the joins themselves; and tatweel, a real character (U+0640) inserted to lengthen a connection.



W3C, Arabic & Persian Layout Requirements, §Text alignment & justification → Kashida. Reproduced under the W3C Document License.
Read right to left. Each row is one word, an arrow, then the same word with a kashida applied: a horizontal connection inside it has been drawn out. No space changed width — the word itself got longer.
ALREQ is careful about limits: too much kashida, or several close together, gives uneven colour, and some typefaces need curved kashidas, which is much harder to implement.


What all six protect is what ALREQ calls colour — even ink density, the property value structure is about. Software that knows only the word-space lever produces bad Arabic.
Direction is not one arrow
Arabic runs right to left, and the page flips with it. But a line is rarely one direction: ALREQ's Writing mode notes that numbers and embedded Latin run left to right inside it. Sorting that out is the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX #9). Text is stored in the order it is spoken; for display the paragraph gets a base direction, is split into directional runs, and the runs are ordered by that direction. Punctuation is neutral and takes direction from its neighbours — or from the base direction when they disagree, which is why a stray bracket lands at the wrong end.
Writing mode adds another turn. ALREQ's Vertical text has Arabic rotated to run along the line on book spines and table headers — and rotated again inside vertically set Chinese, Japanese or Mongolian.
Japanese: no word spaces at all
Chinese and Japanese put no spaces between words, so "don't break inside a word" has nothing to attach to; Typotheque notes a break can fall between any two characters, and hyphens are not used at all. What replaces it is positional. JLREQ's Characters Not Starting a Line forbids beginning a line with a closing bracket, full stop, comma or middle dot; Characters Not Ending a Line forbids ending on an opening bracket. The family of adjustments is kinsokushori.



W3C, Requirements for Japanese Text Layout, Figure 18, §2.3 Vertical Writing Mode and Horizontal Writing Mode. Reproduced under the W3C Document License.
The same sentence twice. Top: vertical mode — characters run down, columns advance right to left. Bottom: horizontal, left to right. Follow the grey arrows.
Now look at the blue cells. Every character fills an identical square, which is why one set of type serves both directions. It is also why "45 to 75 characters per line" cannot be imported: JLREQ specifies a page as a kihon-hanmen, a grid fixed by character size, direction, line length, lines per page and line gap. Characters-per-line advice assumes proportional letters of varying width. There are none here.


JLREQ treats both modes as first-class for the same content, and reports Japan publishes them in roughly equal quantity: newspapers entirely vertical, novels almost so, textbooks mostly horizontal. Leading changes too: Typotheque recommends about 1.7 for CJK against the 1.2 applications default to.
Annotations Latin has no equivalent of


Ruby: the reading, set alongside
Warichu: a note split into two small lines inside the line


W3C, Requirements for Japanese Text Layout, Figures 105 and 145. Reproduced under the W3C Document License.
Left — ruby: small characters attached to base characters to give their reading; when it spells out how to pronounce a kanji it is furigana. JLREQ puts it to the right of the base characters in vertical mode and above them in horizontal mode, and defines three layouts with separate rules — mono-ruby per character, group-ruby across a run, jukugo-ruby for compounds. JLREQ describes ruby as frequently used in modern documents including newspapers: ordinary text, not a specialism.
Right — warichu, an inline cutting note: two lines of smaller characters set inside the body line, splitting it in half. Less frequent, but standard in reference books and travel guides. No Latin device does this.


Rules that do not transfer

Word spacing as the justification lever. One of six mechanisms in Arabic, often the last resort. In CJK the characters sit on a grid, and Typotheque notes CJK text is usually justified precisely because that is more even than shuffling spaces.
Italic as emphasis. JLREQ's Composition of Emphasis Dots gives the Japanese inventory: dots (bouten) beside the characters, a typeface change from Mincho to gothic, colour, enclosing brackets, a line alongside. It calls the typeface change and the brackets the popular ones. Italic is not on the list.
Capitalisation as hierarchy. CSS Fonts 4 calls Latin and Cyrillic "bicameral scripts… that distinguish between upper and lowercase letters". Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Japanese and Chinese have no second case, so all-caps headings, small caps and Title Case do not exist as devices. Size, weight, brackets and grid position carry it instead (Type hierarchy on a page, Visual hierarchy).
Letter-spacing as styling. ILREQ's Letter Spacing is exact: where English spaces every character, Devanagari spaces after each orthographic syllable, which breaks the headline bar across the top of the word. ALREQ's Text spacing says Arabic stretching "does not correspond to letter-spacing in non-cursive scripts" — you extend the baseline, unequally.

Common mistakes

"Right-to-left just means mirroring the layout." The layout does mirror, but the line is mixed-direction and needs the bidi algorithm. Reversing a string is not RTL support.
"We support Arabic, we have the characters." Without contextual shaping you get isolated forms in a row — English printed one letter at a time. ALREQ notes the old "typewriter" fonts reusing one glyph across positions were simplifications, not designs.
"Vertical text is horizontal text rotated." Ideographs and kana stay upright while the line runs downwards. Only embedded Latin is rotated 90°, forced to full width, or set as tate-chu-yoko — a small horizontal cluster inside the vertical line.
"Match the scripts by making them look alike." Typotheque's cautionary case is van Krimpen's Romulus Greek of 1931, now the standard example of Latin-centric misreading.


Before you judge non-Latin type

Which script is it, and is it cursive? If letters should join, check that they do — broken joins are the commonest defect there is.
Is the line mixed-direction? Find a number inside RTL text and check the punctuation landed on the correct side.
If it is CJK, is the text vertical or horizontal — and are the annotations on the side that mode requires?
Ask what the Latin rule you are about to apply depends on. If it needs spaces, case, or letters standing apart, it may not exist here. Looking on purpose transfers; the rules of thumb do not.

              Type anatomy
              The named parts of a letter, and which of them actually decide whether a page is easy to read rather than merely pretty.
            
          
        
          
            
              Measure and line height
              The two settings that decide whether body text is comfortable — how long the lines are, and how far apart. They have to be chosen together.
            
          
        
          
            
              Legibility and readability
              Two different measurements that get treated as one — whether you can tell the characters apart, and whether you can get through a paragraph without effort.
            
          
        
          
            
              Type hierarchy on a page
              How a reader finds their way through a page without being told — by size, weight, space, position and case. Space does more of the work than size does.
            
          
        
          
            
              How to look at an image
              A repeatable way to see what an image is actually doing, instead of only noticing whether you like it.
